title: Heracles: Madness and Service
subtitle: The hero who killed his family — and the sentence that made him

learningObjectives.text: What drives Heracles to his worst act?

main.author: Pseudo-Apollodorus
main.locator: Library 2.4.12, madness, purification, and service; book 2 · chapter 4 · section 12, normalized characters 0-525
main.excerpt: Now it came to pass that after the battle with the Minyans Hercules was driven mad through the jealousy of Hera and flung his own children, whom he had by Megara, and two children of Iphicles into the fire; wherefore he condemned himself to exile, and was purified by Thespius, and repairing to Delphi he inquired of the god where he should dwell. The Pythian priestess then first called him Hercules, for hitherto he was called Alcides. And she told him to dwell in Tiryns, serving Eurystheus for twelve years and to perform

narrativeBlocks.title: Born under a curse
narrativeBlocks.body: Heracles is Zeus's son by the mortal Alcmene — and Hera's hatred begins at his conception. She sends serpents to his cradle (he strangles them) and spends his life hounding the child her husband fathered.

narrativeBlocks.title: The madness sent by Hera
narrativeBlocks.body: At his height — a wife, children, a city — Hera strikes him with madness. In the fog of it he kills his own sons (and in some accounts his wife Megara). When the fog lifts, the man under the hero's skin is a child-killer.

narrativeBlocks.title: The oracle's sentence
narrativeBlocks.body: He seeks purification at Delphi and the answer is service: twelve years under his cousin Eurystheus, a man far beneath him in courage. The greatest hero in Greece takes orders from a coward — that is the price of absolution.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why this story matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Heracles is not a clean hero: he breaks things he loves as often as he saves them. The labours are redemptive precisely because he is not innocent — the Greeks kept both halves, the monster-killer and the man who must be cleansed.

narrativeBlocks.title: The pattern: service as penance
narrativeBlocks.body: Greek heroes repeatedly pay for blood with service (Orestes, Apollo after Python, Heracles). The rule seems to be: the gods don't forgive bloodguilt — they commute it into labour.

quiz.prompt: What drives Heracles to kill his own children?

choices.text: Hera sends a fit of madness on him — the persecution begun at his birth as Zeus's illegitimate son
A poisoned wound drives him to frenzy
He does it knowingly in anger

quiz.explanation: Hera's madness produces the crime — and the labours are the sentence that follows.

choices.text: He is Zeus's son by a mortal woman — her hatred of the child starts at his conception
He refused to worship at her temple
He stole the golden apples from her garden

quiz.explanation: The enmity is dynastic jealousy: every labour he survives is another insult to her pride.
